aldemar.headline: The ten-year touched its highest since 2002 — and the reason was French, Japanese and American debt at once
aldemar.standfirst: Tuesday’s relief in the long end lasted exactly one session. The ten-year spiked to 5.35% in the morning, up nearly eight basis points and its highest since 2002, before closing at 5.29% — a fresh 52-week high — with the thirty-year at 5.671% and the two-year falling again to 4.777%. The fifth steepening in six sessions, and this time the framing was global: rising yields worldwide, record public debt, and France’s index down 1.2% amid mass protests over a budget whose €74.5bn of interest payments exceed its education spending. The September Fed minutes then said the committee expects another hike before year-end. Equities gave back the record: S&P −0.22%, Russell −1.31%, two-thirds of issues lower. In the book PLTR held a gain for a second session, up 1.07% to 194.12 with its low now above Tuesday’s close; AAPL rose 0.91% to its best close since the Ternus news and OKTA was the only holding to fall, at +1.75R. Heat 3.00R against 3.0R, unchanged for a twentieth session.

themes.note: CPI on the 13th now carries more than it did on Tuesday. The Fed's minutes say another hike is coming; two ISM prices indices are accelerating; and core PCE missed to the downside eight days ago. A hot CPI validates the minutes and the long end together, and the thirty-year at 5.671% stops being a term-premium puzzle and becomes an inflation trade. A soft one puts the Fed's stated intention against its own data and leaves the global debt story as the only explanation standing — which is the version with no release to trade against it.

items.html: Tuesday's easing in the long end lasted exactly one session. The ten-year made a fresh 52-week high at 5.29%, up 1.9 basis points, and the thirty-year at 5.671%, up 3.0 — after the ten-year spiked to 5.35% in the morning, up nearly eight basis points and its highest since 2002, before half-retracing. The two-year fell again, to 4.777%. That is the fifth steepening in six sessions.

And this is not an American story. The AP wire tied the move to rising bond yields worldwide, high inflation and growing government debt. France's index fell 1.2% amid mass demonstrations over its budget, with public debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027 and projected interest payments of €74.5bn — more than the country spends on education. The IMF's Georgieva cited record public debt; Ray Dalio warned of a US debt crisis.

The September FOMC minutes said another hike, not a cut. Released at 2pm, they show the committee anticipates one more increase before year-end without specifying 28 October or 9 December. The market moved October odds to roughly 20%. Equities gave back Tuesday's record: S&P −0.22%, Nasdaq −0.22%, Dow −0.66%, and the Russell −1.31%, with over two-thirds of US issues lower.

recap.note: The book went the other way entirely. Only OKTA fell, 0.31%. GOOG has crossed +1R — the first position to do so since OKTA crossed it on 29 September, and the only one with a standing question attached to that threshold. changed.title: The yield story turned out to be a sovereign-debt story, and not only America's
changed.note: 1. Tuesday's relief lasted one session, and the framing changed. The ten-year spiked to 5.35% in the morning, its highest since 2002, and closed at 5.29% — a fresh 52-week high — while the two-year fell again. That is the fifth steepening in six sessions. What is new is where the pressure is coming from: the move was global. Asian and European equities fell, France's index lost 1.2% amid nationwide demonstrations over its budget, the IMF's Georgieva pointed at record public debt and Ray Dalio warned about America's. France is the clean illustration — debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027, the ten-year OAT up roughly 139 basis points in a year, and €74.5bn of projected interest payments exceeding the education budget. Several governments are being repriced at once. No central bank's reaction function explains that; the supply of paper and the premium demanded to hold it does.

weekly.headline: Three data points argued for lower yields and the long end finished higher — which leaves only supply and term premium
weekly.standfirst: Consumer confidence hit a twelve-year low on Tuesday, core PCE missed to the downside on Wednesday, and Friday’s payrolls came in at 29,000 against 90,000 expected with 60,000 revised out of the prior two months — and the long end rose on all three. October hike odds collapsed from 64% to 16%, the two-year fell to 4.84%, and the ten-year still finished at 5.28% with the thirty-year having touched a 24-year high. There is no Fed-path explanation left for that; supply and term premium are what remain, and a cut cures neither. The largest move on the board says the same thing: gold fell 3.30% to $4,140.19 in a week it should have risen on every headline. The index registered almost none of it — S&P −0.27%, Nasdaq +0.45%, Dow −1.26% — while the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels, diesel first, and crude fell to $91.11. In the book nothing was opened, closed or moved for a fifth consecutive week: OKTA rose 8.35% to a fresh 52-week high while PLTR fell 0.49% on no news at all, and AAPL lost 2.16% on a management restructuring and a named AI threat. Heat 3.00R against 3.0R, unchanged for seventeen sessions.

sections.html:
Sigma (σ) measures a move against that instrument’s own recent behaviour, not against zero. Here it is measured on weekly changes over the last twenty weeks, so one sigma is an ordinary week and two is a week bigger than roughly 95% of the last twenty.

The largest move on the board was gold, down 3.30% to $4,140.19, at 1.14 sigma. Hold that against what the week actually contained: consumer confidence at a twelve-year low on Tuesday, core PCE missing to the downside on Wednesday, and payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 on Friday with 60,000 revised out of the prior two months. Gold is the asset that should rise on every one of those. It fell three and a half percent, and it has now fallen for two consecutive weeks. There is one explanation that fits: the long end would not come down, and a non-yielding asset cannot compete with a 5.28% ten-year.

The second-largest move was the Dow, down 1.26% at 1.05 sigma, or 651.66 points. The rest of the board barely moved on a weekly basis: Nasdaq +0.45%, S&P −0.27%, Russell −0.16%, and crude −1.92% from $92.89 to $91.11. So the index did nothing for a second consecutive week while the spread between its components widened again: Nasdaq over Dow by 1.71 points in five sessions, after 5.2 points in the quarter just ended. That rotation is the market, and the S&P is not measuring it.

The rate story is now a thesis rather than an observation. Four data points landed this week and three of them argued for lower yields. Tuesday: consumer confidence 81.9, down 6.7 points against roughly 90 expected, the weakest since 2014, and job openings down 256,000 to 7.08m — and the thirty-year rose to 5.6206%, its highest since June 2002. Wednesday: core PCE 3.0% against 3.3% expected and headline 3.4% against 3.7% — and the two-year fell a basis point while the thirty-year rose five, widening two-to-thirty by roughly six basis points on good inflation news. Friday: the weakest payroll print of the cycle, October hike odds collapsing from 64% to 16% — and the ten-year rose about four basis points to 5.28%.

Only Thursday behaved conventionally, and it needed help: the ten-year ran to 5.3338% intraday, its highest since 2002, before closing lower on an ISM headline of 54.5 against 55.0 expected — though the same report showed prices paid up 6.8 points to 77.9, new orders at 55.3 and employment at 52.7. So the one session the long end fell, it fell on a headline whose internals pointed the other way. Three-for-four is not a coincidence. There is no Fed-path explanation left: the market has all but cancelled the next hike and is still demanding more to hold duration. That leaves supply and term premium, and a rate cut does not cure either.

And equities finished the week by rallying into it anyway. Friday's session was the only broad one in five — Nasdaq +1.19%, Russell +0.94%, S&P +0.73%, the VIX down 6.59% to 15.31, Nvidia at a record $5.72tn. The question this book cannot answer and does not need to answer this week is whether earnings can carry a five-percent curve. The first data on that arrives 28 October, when Alphabet reports on the same day the Fed decides.

A fifth consecutive week without a decision, and one position carried all of it

Nothing was opened, closed, trimmed or moved. Heat is 3.00R against a 3.0R cap, exactly where it has been since 14 September — seventeen sessions — because heat is set by entries, stops and sizes and none of those changed. Checked against the lowest low of all five sessions rather than any close, the nearest any holding came to a stop was AAPL at 7.31%, on Thursday's 325.81. No stop was ever in question.

The week's entire result is OKTA. It rose +8.35% across the five sessions, from 195.19 to 211.49, making a fresh 52-week high at 216.59 on Friday before closing red. The other two holdings fell: PLTR −0.49% and AAPL −2.16%. The book gained $8.00 on the week and OKTA contributed $16.30 of it — more than the whole, because the rest was a drag. On $689.14 of committed capital that is +1.16% for the week, against the S&P's −0.27% and the Dow's −1.26%.

What OKTA was paid for is specific and worth restating. The street repriced it wholesale after Oktane: Morgan Stanley to $245 on Tuesday and Scotiabank to $245 the week before, Stephens $240, DA Davidson and Truist $235, BMO $230, Oppenheimer $227, Citizens $225, Bank of America $220. Four consecutive up sessions Monday to Thursday took it through the 206.64 close and 212.39 high that had capped it, undoing Bernstein's 25 September sector downgrade entirely. The bear check comes from Scotiabank's own survey work: interest in the AI-agent products is strong but only 10% of customers surveyed had signed contracts, and with three-to-nine-month sales cycles the revenue starts in fiscal 2028. Everything above $220 is being paid for something not yet in the numbers.

PLTR did nothing for four sessions and then was sold into a rally. Down 0.49% across the week with no company news on any day, and on Friday it opened 193.03, reached 194.78 and closed 188.75, on its low, while the Nasdaq rose 1.19%. Context worth holding: Palantir rose 60.32% in Q3 and this position captured almost none of it, because the 27 August entry at 184.45 came late in the move; the stock remains about 10% below its 207.52 high. The 2 November print is expected to show whether US commercial revenue has overtaken government — in Q2 commercial grew 149% to $764m against government's 90% to $809m.

AAPL was the week's worst holding and the reason is structural. Down 2.16% from 341.07 to 333.69, with a 2.66% fall on Tuesday that has only partly come back. Two pieces of news, one story: chief executive John Ternus, four weeks into the job, is cutting layers of middle management and eliminating engineering programme manager roles affecting roughly half a dozen directors; and Bank of America's Wamsi Mohan, keeping his Buy, warned that Meta's Muse — now wired into Shopify, Expedia and PayPal — could take product discovery, referrals and transaction initiation even if Apple keeps selling the handset. The stock has recovered $4.29 of a nine-dollar fall in three sessions. This is a slower and larger risk than any iPhone cycle, and the first read on Ternus is 29 October.

And the quarter turned inside the week. Q3 closed on Wednesday at +17.04, or +0.84R — September's stops against the open book as it stood that afternoon — compared with the S&P's +2.0% for the quarter and the Dow's −2.7%. Q4 began on Thursday with nothing realised, and two sessions in that has not changed: the +44.79 in the column is the open book crossing a date, not a Q4 return. The number that matters is not the total but its shape: 64% of the open gain sits in a single position opened thirteen sessions ago, and there is no catalyst on anything held until 28 October.

Three data points argued for lower yields and the long end finished higher

1. The week settled the rate question in the least convenient direction. A twelve-year low in consumer confidence, a downside core PCE miss, and the weakest payroll print of the cycle with 60,000 revised out of the prior two months — and over those three sessions the long end rose every time. The front end did exactly what it should: the two-year is at 4.84% and October hike odds fell from 64% to 16%. The back end ignored it. When the curve steepens on good inflation news and weak growth news in the same week, the marginal buyer of duration is not pricing the economy — it is pricing the supply of paper and the premium required to hold it. Kashkari's line on Thursday, that inflation is still too high at around 3%, closes the other escape route: the committee is not reading 3.0% core as permission to ease. Three of this book's holdings are long-duration growth names priced off that number.

2. The AI-regulation trade was tested and failed inside a day and a half. Wednesday's White House accord — Pichai, Zuckerberg, Huang, Amodei, Brockman, Musk, four layers of controls, an independent external auditor, an independent board committee, and no enforcement mechanism, which Trump called morally binding — produced a 3% mega-cap rally that was entirely sold into the quarter-end close. Thursday Alphabet reached 350.09 and closed 334.93, below where it had traded before the accord existed. A voluntary agreement turns out to be worth nothing to the equity, and the market needed thirty-six hours to decide. For Alphabet it sits directly against Tuesday's EU appeal: Brussels is setting dates and Washington is setting intentions, and only one of those appears in a model.

3. The G7 opened the reserves, which is what happens when diplomacy stalls. On Friday the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels over four months through the IEA — roughly 830,000 a day — with diesel prioritised inside 20 days, extra refinery runs, and commitments not to restrict energy trade between members. Macron led it off an overnight call with Trump about potential US diesel export restrictions, which identifies the real fear as a winter diesel shortage rather than the crude price. Set that against the week's diplomatic record: an offer rejected on Saturday, a reply delivered through Qatar on Wednesday whose contents nobody will state, and silence since. Crude ended the week −1.92%. Nine sessions of headlines moved the price approximately nowhere, and the policy response was to stop waiting.

sections.right: crude −1.92% · the G7 opens the reserves
sections.html:
An offer rejected, a reply delivered through Qatar, and then the reserves

The week opened with a rejection. Trump turned down Iran's seven-point proposal — terms that asked the United States to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz — saying the US has total control of the Hormuz Strait and that the war would end very soon. A vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile in the strait on Monday; the fire was extinguished with no casualties. On Tuesday Revolutionary Guard spokesman Gen. Mohebbi called on the United States to leave the region and disputed that the waterway had been restored at all.

Then the channel worked, quietly. On Wednesday Washington's reply reached Tehran through Qatari mediation. Foreign Minister Araghchi took delivery and briefed the cabinet; spokeswoman Mohajerani declined to disclose the contents or say what Iran intends. Nothing has been added by either side in the three days since, while Iran has threatened new strikes as it waits. A channel that carries a formal reply and then goes silent is usually a channel doing work — but it is not producing anything a price can trade.

So the week's real oil event was a policy decision, not a diplomatic one. The G7's 100 million barrels over four months, diesel first, came with officials cautioning that strategic crude does not become diesel without refinery capacity — so the announcement may do more for sentiment than for supply. Crude's week: $92.89 to $89.30 on Tuesday, back to $92.87 on Thursday, and $91.11 on Friday. Down 1.92% over five sessions and inside the range it has held for a fortnight.

For the book the conclusion is firmer than it was a week ago. At $91 crude is neither pushing the long end up nor pulling it down. The oil channel that dominated the middle of September has closed, and the rate problem now has to be explained by ISM internals, auction supply and term premium. What would reopen it is another strike on Yanbu — the terminal Aramco's pipeline bypass routes to — or a formal collapse of the Qatari channel. Neither happened this week.

sections.right: thin data · then everything on 28 October
sections.html:
Nothing of consequence until CPI, and nothing from the companies until the 28th

CPISeptember CPI — the only print before the Fed with the weight to move a five-percent curveTue2026-10-13
FOMCFed decision — October hike odds are 16%; the long end is not waiting for the answerWed2026-10-28
GOOGAlphabet Q3 earnings — the first read on $195-205bn of capex and on Suncatcher, the same day as the FedWed2026-10-28
AAPLApple Q4 earnings — the first iPhone 18 quarter and the first read on TernusThu2026-10-29

The coming week is thin and that matters more than it sounds. Payrolls was the last first-tier release for a fortnight; the next thing heavy enough to move the long end is September CPI on 13 October. Until then the curve is left with auctions, supply and positioning — which is exactly the regime that produced this week's result and the hardest one to forecast, because there is no release to react to. Expect the index to drift and the dispersion to stay underneath it, as it has for two weeks.

Then four empty weeks and everything at once. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple the 29th, Palantir 2 November, Okta in early December. Three of this book's holdings report inside five sessions at the end of the month, immediately after a rate decision. Nothing needs a decision before then.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the long end keeps rising without a data excuse — that is now the thesis rather than a curiosity, and the test is the auction calendar. Whether Friday's rotation inside the book holds: the two names that had led the week were both sold into a 1.19% Nasdaq rally while the two laggards were bought, which is either a one-day funding effect or the beginning of something. And whether the Nasdaq-over-Dow spread keeps widening, because this book owns three names on one side of it and nothing on the other.

The standing discipline. Heat is at 3.00R against a 3.0R cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable whatever it returns. All 3 holdings are green, the nearest any came to a stop in five sessions was 7.3% on the week's lowest low, and there is no catalyst for four weeks. Seventeen sessions without a change in this book — the fifth consecutive week in which the right decision was made by not being made.

themes.note: CPI on the 13th now carries more than it did on Tuesday. The Fed's minutes say another hike is coming; two ISM prices indices are accelerating; and core PCE missed to the downside eight days ago. A hot CPI validates the minutes and the long end together, and the thirty-year at 5.671% stops being a term-premium puzzle and becomes an inflation trade. A soft one puts the Fed's stated intention against its own data and leaves the global debt story as the only explanation standing — which is the version with no release to trade against it.

world.right: a hurricane replaces the war premium · crude $90.12
world.title: Twenty-five percent of Gulf output is shut in, and not because of Iran
world.note: Oil rose on weather. WTI gained 2.68% to $90.12 and Brent moved toward $102 with about a quarter of Gulf of Mexico oil output shut in ahead of Tropical Storm Isaias, which is forecast to reach the US Gulf coast as a hurricane early Saturday. Chevron, Shell and BP have pulled workers from platforms; Shell declared evacuation from six. This is the first session in a month where the marginal driver of the crude price had nothing to do with the Strait of Hormuz.

items.html: Tuesday's easing in the long end lasted exactly one session. The ten-year made a fresh 52-week high at 5.29%, up 1.9 basis points, and the thirty-year at 5.671%, up 3.0 — after the ten-year spiked to 5.35% in the morning, up nearly eight basis points and its highest since 2002, before half-retracing. The two-year fell again, to 4.777%. That is the fifth steepening in six sessions.

And this is not an American story. The AP wire tied the move to rising bond yields worldwide, high inflation and growing government debt. France's index fell 1.2% amid mass demonstrations over its budget, with public debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027 and projected interest payments of €74.5bn — more than the country spends on education. The IMF's Georgieva cited record public debt; Ray Dalio warned of a US debt crisis.

The September FOMC minutes said another hike, not a cut. Released at 2pm, they show the committee anticipates one more increase before year-end without specifying 28 October or 9 December. The market moved October odds to roughly 20%. Equities gave back Tuesday's record: S&P −0.22%, Nasdaq −0.22%, Dow −0.66%, and the Russell −1.31%, with over two-thirds of US issues lower.

recap.note: The book went the other way entirely. It added +5.15 on a day the index fell, because three of the four names rose: GOOG +0.81% to 347.37, a third consecutive closing high; AAPL +0.91% to 336.67, its best close since the Ternus repricing; PLTR +1.07% to 194.12, a second straight held gain. Only OKTA fell, 0.31%. GOOG has crossed +1R — the first position to do so since OKTA crossed it on 29 September, and the only one with a standing question attached to that threshold. Nothing came near a stop; heat is unchanged for a twentieth session.

markets.title: Russell 2000 drops 1.3% — the board's largest move, though it stopped short of two sigma
markets.note: Crude led the board and the Russell was the equity story. WTI's 2.68% rise was 0.90σ and the Russell's 1.31% fall 1.74σ — a second consecutive decline and much the largest in the equity complex. The S&P's 0.22% was 0.36σ, the Nasdaq's 0.26σ and the Dow's 0.66% 1.12σ. The index barely moved and the small-cap index fell more than one percent, which is the same pattern as Tuesday with the volume turned up.

changed.title: The yield story turned out to be a sovereign-debt story, and not only America's
changed.note: 1. Tuesday's relief lasted one session, and the framing changed. The ten-year spiked to 5.35% in the morning, its highest since 2002, and closed at 5.29% — a fresh 52-week high — while the two-year fell again. That is the fifth steepening in six sessions. What is new is where the pressure is coming from: the move was global. Asian and European equities fell, France's index lost 1.2% amid nationwide demonstrations over its budget, the IMF's Georgieva pointed at record public debt and Ray Dalio warned about America's. France is the clean illustration — debt heading for 121.7% of GDP in 2027, the ten-year OAT up roughly 139 basis points in a year, and €74.5bn of projected interest payments exceeding the education budget. Several governments are being repriced at once. No central bank's reaction function explains that; the supply of paper and the premium demanded to hold it does.

weekly.headline: Three data points argued for lower yields and the long end finished higher — which leaves only supply and term premium
weekly.standfirst: Consumer confidence hit a twelve-year low on Tuesday, core PCE missed to the downside on Wednesday, and Friday’s payrolls came in at 29,000 against 90,000 expected with 60,000 revised out of the prior two months — and the long end rose on all three. October hike odds collapsed from 64% to 16%, the two-year fell to 4.84%, and the ten-year still finished at 5.28% with the thirty-year having touched a 24-year high. There is no Fed-path explanation left for that; supply and term premium are what remain, and a cut cures neither. The largest move on the board says the same thing: gold fell 3.30% to $4,140.19 in a week it should have risen on every headline. The index registered almost none of it — S&P −0.27%, Nasdaq +0.45%, Dow −1.26% — while the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels, diesel first, and crude fell to $91.11. In the book nothing was opened, closed or moved for a fifth consecutive week: OKTA rose 8.35% to a fresh 52-week high while GOOG fell 0.21% through two regulatory stories and a rocket launch, and AAPL lost 2.16% on a management restructuring and a named AI threat. Heat 3.05R against 3.0R, unchanged for seventeen sessions.

The largest move on the board was gold, down 3.30% to $4,140.19, at 1.14 sigma. Hold that against what the week actually contained: consumer confidence at a twelve-year low on Tuesday, core PCE missing to the downside on Wednesday, and payrolls at 29,000 against 90,000 on Friday with 60,000 revised out of the prior two months. Gold is the asset that should rise on every one of those. It fell three and a half percent, and it has now fallen for two consecutive weeks. There is one explanation that fits: the long end would not come down, and a non-yielding asset cannot compete with a 5.28% ten-year.

The second-largest move was the Dow, down 1.26% at 1.05 sigma, or 651.66 points. The rest of the board barely moved on a weekly basis: Nasdaq +0.45%, S&P −0.27%, Russell −0.16%, and crude −1.92% from $92.89 to $91.11. So the index did nothing for a second consecutive week while the spread between its components widened again: Nasdaq over Dow by 1.71 points in five sessions, after 5.2 points in the quarter just ended. That rotation is the market, and the S&P is not measuring it.

The rate story is now a thesis rather than an observation. Four data points landed this week and three of them argued for lower yields. Tuesday: consumer confidence 81.9, down 6.7 points against roughly 90 expected, the weakest since 2014, and job openings down 256,000 to 7.08m — and the thirty-year rose to 5.6206%, its highest since June 2002. Wednesday: core PCE 3.0% against 3.3% expected and headline 3.4% against 3.7% — and the two-year fell a basis point while the thirty-year rose five, widening two-to-thirty by roughly six basis points on good inflation news. Friday: the weakest payroll print of the cycle, October hike odds collapsing from 64% to 16% — and the ten-year rose about four basis points to 5.28%.

Only Thursday behaved conventionally, and it needed help: the ten-year ran to 5.3338% intraday, its highest since 2002, before closing lower on an ISM headline of 54.5 against 55.0 expected — though the same report showed prices paid up 6.8 points to 77.9, new orders at 55.3 and employment at 52.7. So the one session the long end fell, it fell on a headline whose internals pointed the other way. Three-for-four is not a coincidence. There is no Fed-path explanation left: the market has all but cancelled the next hike and is still demanding more to hold duration. That leaves supply and term premium, and a rate cut does not cure either.

And equities finished the week by rallying into it anyway. Friday's session was the only broad one in five — Nasdaq +1.19%, Russell +0.94%, S&P +0.73%, the VIX down 6.59% to 15.31, Nvidia at a record $5.72tn. The question this book cannot answer and does not need to answer this week is whether earnings can carry a five-percent curve. The first data on that arrives 28 October, when Alphabet reports on the same day the Fed decides.

A fifth consecutive week without a decision, and one position carried all of it

Nothing was opened, closed, trimmed or moved. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap (2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position), exactly where it has been since 14 September — seventeen sessions — because heat is set by entries, stops and sizes and none of those changed. Checked against the lowest low of all five sessions rather than any close, the nearest any holding came to a stop was AAPL at 7.54%, on Thursday's 325.81. No stop was ever in question.

The week's entire result is OKTA. It rose +8.35% across the five sessions, from 195.19 to 211.49, making a fresh 52-week high at 216.59 on Friday before closing red. The other two holdings fell: GOOG −0.21% and AAPL −2.16%. The book gained $8.19 on the week and OKTA contributed $16.30 of it — more than the whole, because the rest was a drag. On $830.56 of committed capital that is +0.99% for the week, against the S&P's −0.27% and the Dow's −1.26%.

What OKTA was paid for is specific and worth restating. The street repriced it wholesale after Oktane: Morgan Stanley to $245 on Tuesday and Scotiabank to $245 the week before, Stephens $240, DA Davidson and Truist $235, BMO $230, Oppenheimer $227, Citizens $225, Bank of America $220. Four consecutive up sessions Monday to Thursday took it through the 206.64 close and 212.39 high that had capped it, undoing Bernstein's 25 September sector downgrade entirely. The bear check comes from Scotiabank's own survey work: interest in the AI-agent products is strong but only 10% of customers surveyed had signed contracts, and with three-to-nine-month sales cycles the revenue starts in fiscal 2028. Everything above $220 is being paid for something not yet in the numbers.

GOOG had a week of violence that netted to nothing. Down 0.21% across the five sessions, but the path was 339.16, 337.32, 340.74, 334.93, 340.35, with an intraday high of 350.09 on Thursday and a low of 332.65 the same day. Two separate stories drove it: Tuesday's appeal against two EU orders — search-data sharing from January 2027, Android opening the year after — and Wednesday's White House AI accord, signed with Zuckerberg, Huang, Amodei, Brockman and Musk, four layers of audit and no enforcement. The accord was worth 3% for a day and a half and then nothing. Thursday it launched Project Suncatcher, TPUs on a Falcon 9, and fell 1.71% through it.

AAPL was the week's worst holding and the reason is structural. Down 2.16% from 341.07 to 333.69, with a 2.66% fall on Tuesday that has only partly come back. Two pieces of news, one story: chief executive John Ternus, four weeks into the job, is cutting layers of middle management and eliminating engineering programme manager roles affecting roughly half a dozen directors; and Bank of America's Wamsi Mohan, keeping his Buy, warned that Meta's Muse — now wired into Shopify, Expedia and PayPal — could take product discovery, referrals and transaction initiation even if Apple keeps selling the handset. The stock has recovered $4.29 of a nine-dollar fall in three sessions. This is a slower and larger risk than any iPhone cycle, and the first read on Ternus is 29 October.

And the quarter turned inside the week. Q3 closed on Wednesday at +12.31, or +0.58R — September's stops against the open book as it stood that afternoon — compared with the S&P's +2.0% for the quarter and the Dow's −2.7%. Q4 began on Thursday with nothing realised, and two sessions in that has not changed: the +54.97 in the column is the open book crossing a date, not a Q4 return. The number that matters is not the total but its shape: 52% of the open gain sits in a single position opened thirteen sessions ago, and there is no catalyst on anything held until 28 October.

Three data points argued for lower yields and the long end finished higher

1. The week settled the rate question in the least convenient direction. A twelve-year low in consumer confidence, a downside core PCE miss, and the weakest payroll print of the cycle with 60,000 revised out of the prior two months — and over those three sessions the long end rose every time. The front end did exactly what it should: the two-year is at 4.84% and October hike odds fell from 64% to 16%. The back end ignored it. When the curve steepens on good inflation news and weak growth news in the same week, the marginal buyer of duration is not pricing the economy — it is pricing the supply of paper and the premium required to hold it. Kashkari's line on Thursday, that inflation is still too high at around 3%, closes the other escape route: the committee is not reading 3.0% core as permission to ease. Three of this book's holdings are long-duration growth names priced off that number.

2. The AI-regulation trade was tested and failed inside a day and a half. Wednesday's White House accord — Pichai, Zuckerberg, Huang, Amodei, Brockman, Musk, four layers of controls, an independent external auditor, an independent board committee, and no enforcement mechanism, which Trump called morally binding — produced a 3% mega-cap rally that was entirely sold into the quarter-end close. Thursday Alphabet reached 350.09 and closed 334.93, below where it had traded before the accord existed. A voluntary agreement turns out to be worth nothing to the equity, and the market needed thirty-six hours to decide. For Alphabet it sits directly against Tuesday's EU appeal: Brussels is setting dates and Washington is setting intentions, and only one of those appears in a model.

3. The G7 opened the reserves, which is what happens when diplomacy stalls. On Friday the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels over four months through the IEA — roughly 830,000 a day — with diesel prioritised inside 20 days, extra refinery runs, and commitments not to restrict energy trade between members. Macron led it off an overnight call with Trump about potential US diesel export restrictions, which identifies the real fear as a winter diesel shortage rather than the crude price. Set that against the week's diplomatic record: an offer rejected on Saturday, a reply delivered through Qatar on Wednesday whose contents nobody will state, and silence since. Crude ended the week −1.92%. Nine sessions of headlines moved the price approximately nowhere, and the policy response was to stop waiting.

sections.right: crude −1.92% · the G7 opens the reserves
sections.html:
An offer rejected, a reply delivered through Qatar, and then the reserves

The week opened with a rejection. Trump turned down Iran's seven-point proposal — terms that asked the United States to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz — saying the US has total control of the Hormuz Strait and that the war would end very soon. A vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile in the strait on Monday; the fire was extinguished with no casualties. On Tuesday Revolutionary Guard spokesman Gen. Mohebbi called on the United States to leave the region and disputed that the waterway had been restored at all.

Then the channel worked, quietly. On Wednesday Washington's reply reached Tehran through Qatari mediation. Foreign Minister Araghchi took delivery and briefed the cabinet; spokeswoman Mohajerani declined to disclose the contents or say what Iran intends. Nothing has been added by either side in the three days since, while Iran has threatened new strikes as it waits. A channel that carries a formal reply and then goes silent is usually a channel doing work — but it is not producing anything a price can trade.

So the week's real oil event was a policy decision, not a diplomatic one. The G7's 100 million barrels over four months, diesel first, came with officials cautioning that strategic crude does not become diesel without refinery capacity — so the announcement may do more for sentiment than for supply. Crude's week: $92.89 to $89.30 on Tuesday, back to $92.87 on Thursday, and $91.11 on Friday. Down 1.92% over five sessions and inside the range it has held for a fortnight.

For the book the conclusion is firmer than it was a week ago. At $91 crude is neither pushing the long end up nor pulling it down. The oil channel that dominated the middle of September has closed, and the rate problem now has to be explained by ISM internals, auction supply and term premium. What would reopen it is another strike on Yanbu — the terminal Aramco's pipeline bypass routes to — or a formal collapse of the Qatari channel. Neither happened this week.

The coming week is thin and that matters more than it sounds. Payrolls was the last first-tier release for a fortnight; the next thing heavy enough to move the long end is September CPI on 13 October. Until then the curve is left with auctions, supply and positioning — which is exactly the regime that produced this week's result and the hardest one to forecast, because there is no release to react to. Expect the index to drift and the dispersion to stay underneath it, as it has for two weeks.

Then four empty weeks and everything at once. Alphabet reports 28 October on the same day the Fed decides, Apple the 29th, Palantir 2 November, Okta in early December. Three of this book's holdings report inside five sessions at the end of the month, immediately after a rate decision. Nothing needs a decision before then.

Three things to watch through the gap. Whether the long end keeps rising without a data excuse — that is now the thesis rather than a curiosity, and the test is the auction calendar. Whether Friday's rotation inside the book holds: the two names that had led the week were both sold into a 1.19% Nasdaq rally while the two laggards were bought, which is either a one-day funding effect or the beginning of something. And whether the Nasdaq-over-Dow spread keeps widening, because this book owns three names on one side of it and nothing on the other.

The standing discipline. Heat is at 3.05R against a 3.0R cap, so nothing on the screener is actionable whatever it returns. All 3 holdings are green, the nearest any came to a stop in five sessions was 7.5% on the week's lowest low, and there is no catalyst for four weeks. Seventeen sessions without a change in this book — the fifth consecutive week in which the right decision was made by not being made.
